newsitem.title: ITALY: Envoy Vranitzky urges Albanians to vote en masse.
newsitem.headline: Envoy Vranitzky urges Albanians to vote en masse.

text.p: European envoy Franz Vranitzky appealed to all Albanian voters on Friday to turn out for Sunday's early general election and to armed gangs to lay down their weapons for the sake of the country.

Speaking in Rome after a pre-election visit to the troubled Balkan state, he said it was crucial for Albania's future that balloting should take place in such a way as to ensure that the outcome would be respected at home and abroad.
He said Albania's squabbling parties had undertaken to accept the result but added: "Knowing Albania...they might have some doubts, especially should they not win."
Vranitzky, a former Austrian chancellor, is envoy to Albania for the Organisation for Security and Cooperation in Europe (OSCE).
The body is supervising the election and has sent several hundred observers, who will be guarded by soldiers from a 7,000 strong Italian-led multinational protection force.

Foreign Minister Lamberto Dini of Italy, the country most involved in Albania, said he was reasonably satisfied that the presence of the observers and troops would ensure that the elections would be properly conducted and scrutinised.
But Vranitzky told a joint news conference that a high turnout was of great importance to the credibility of the exercise.
"I appeal to them (the Albanian people) that they should participate in the election," he said.
"Should they not participate in the election, then they run the risk that decisions are being taken that are not just in their own interest," he said.
The elections follow months of lawlessness sparked by the crash of a string of shady investment funds in Albania, Europe's poorest country.
The electoral campaign has been waged against the backdrop of increasing anarchy and violence, particularly in the south of the country, which remains largely outside government control.
Vranitzky said the activity of armed gangs was one of his main worries for the safe and proper conduct of the election.
"I should extend the appeal to those who carry weapons and use them to stop that in the interests of their own country and the future of their country," he said.
"The gun in the hand of some people, a few people, would definitely not be the future of Albania," he said.
The snap election was called to restore some measure of stability in formerly communist Albania after the establishment in March of an interim unity government made up of 10 parties.
The vote is being held 13 months after Albania's third multi-party elections since the collapse of communism in 1990.
International observers said the 1996 vote, which won President Sali Berisha's right-leaning Democrats 122 of the 140 parliamentary seats, was subject to manipulation and voter intimidation.
